jianbing.title: Jianbing (煎饼): China's Breakfast Crepe, Explained
jianbing.description: China's breakfast crepe, explained: batter, egg, crispy cracker, fermented bean paste. How to order one and eat it before it goes soft.
jianbing.whatIsIt: Jianbing is a Chinese breakfast crepe: a thin batter spread on a hot griddle, cracked with an egg, brushed with fermented bean paste and chili, then folded around a crispy wonton cracker and scallions.
jianbing.howToSay: jiān bǐng - 2 syllables, said roughly like jyen-bing (the e is short, as in 'uh').
jianbing.alsoSpelled: jian bing · jianbing · jiangbing · jian bings · 煎饼
jianbing.inEnglish: In English it is usually called a Chinese crepe, a Chinese breakfast crepe, or a savoury pancake.
jianbing.calories: About 400-500 kcal per crepe. The egg, the fried cracker, and the sauce make it a full breakfast rather than a light snack.
jianbing.originShort: Shandong province, over 2,000 years ago; the Beijing egg-and-cracker version took shape when the snack moved north.
jianbing.firstTimer: Yes - mild by default, cheap (¥5-15), and sold on almost every morning street corner.

tanghulu.title: Tanghulu (糖葫芦): Candied Hawthorn Skewers, Explained
tanghulu.description: Candied hawthorn skewers, explained: what tanghulu tastes like, why it is a winter-only snack, what it costs, and where to buy the good stuff in Beijing.
tanghulu.whatIsIt: Tanghulu is skewered fruit - classically sour hawthorn berries - dipped in a hard, glassy sugar glaze that cracks when you bite through it.
tanghulu.howToSay: táng hú lú - 3 syllables, said roughly like tahng-hoo-loo.
tanghulu.alsoSpelled: tang hulu · tanghulu · tang hu lu · 糖葫芦
tanghulu.inEnglish: In English it is called candied hawthorn skewers, candied fruit on a stick, or sometimes 'Chinese candy apples' - not accurate, but it is the comparison people reach for.
tanghulu.calories: About 120-180 kcal per skewer, and almost all of that is the sugar shell.
tanghulu.originShort: Song Dynasty (960-1279), when hawthorn simmered in sugar was prescribed as medicine and then became a palace favourite.
tanghulu.firstTimer: Yes - but buy it in winter (October to March) and eat it within minutes, because the sugar shell softens fast in warm air.

xiaolongbao.title: Xiaolongbao (小笼包): Shanghai Soup Dumplings, Explained
xiaolongbao.description: Shanghai soup dumplings, explained: how they are made, how to eat them without burning your tongue, what they cost, and the Shanghai shops worth queueing for.
xiaolongbao.whatIsIt: Xiaolongbao are Shanghai's soup dumplings: thin-skinned steamed parcels of minced pork and jellied broth that melts into hot soup as they cook.
xiaolongbao.howToSay: xiǎo lóng bāo - 3 syllables, said roughly like shyow-long-bao.
xiaolongbao.alsoSpelled: xiao long bao · xiaolongbao · xiao long bao · 小笼包 / 小籠包
xiaolongbao.inEnglish: In English they are called soup dumplings, Shanghai soup dumplings, or steamed soup buns.
xiaolongbao.calories: About 40-60 kcal each, so a standard steamer of six works out to roughly 250-350 kcal.
xiaolongbao.originShort: Nanxiang, a suburb of Shanghai, in the 1870s - invented by a restaurateur named Huang Mingxian.
xiaolongbao.firstTimer: Yes, but eat them carefully: lift by the pinched top, bite a small hole first, let the broth cool for a few seconds, and never bite straight in.

chuanchuan.title: Chuan Chuan (串串): Sichuan Skewer Hot Pot, Explained
chuanchuan.description: Sichuan skewer hot pot, explained: pick your sticks, they boil them in spicy broth, and you pay per skewer. Prices and where to eat it in Chengdu.
chuanchuan.whatIsIt: Chuan chuan is Sichuan skewer hot pot: you pick meat, vegetables, and tofu on sticks from a display, the cook boils them in spicy broth, and you pay by the skewer at the end.
chuanchuan.howToSay: chuàn chuàn - 2 identical syllables, said roughly like chwan-chwan.
chuanchuan.alsoSpelled: chuan chuan · chuanchuan · chuanchuanr · 串串
chuanchuan.inEnglish: In English it is called skewer hot pot, Sichuan skewer hot pot, or simply 'hot pot on sticks'.
chuanchuan.calories: Entirely down to how many skewers you take. Vegetable sticks are light; meat, tofu skin, and quail eggs add up quickly, so a typical solo meal of 20-40 sticks is hard to price in calories.
chuanchuan.originShort: Chengdu street stalls in the 1980s, as a cheap solo alternative to table hot pot.
chuanchuan.firstTimer: Yes - it is the easiest way to try Sichuan hot pot alone, because you pay per stick (¥0.5-3 each) and can stop whenever you like.

roujiamo.title: Roujiamo (肉夹馍): Xi'an's Chinese Meat Burger, Explained
roujiamo.description: The Chinese hamburger, explained: pork belly braised for hours, stuffed into a crisp flatbread. What it costs in Xi'an, how to order it, and where to go.
roujiamo.whatIsIt: Roujiamo is Xi'an's signature sandwich: pork belly braised for hours in soy sauce and warm spices, chopped, and stuffed into a crisp-edged flatbread.
roujiamo.howToSay: ròu jiā mó - 3 syllables, said roughly like roe-jyah-mwaw.
roujiamo.alsoSpelled: rou jia mo · roujiamo · rougamo · 肉夹馍
roujiamo.inEnglish: In English it is usually called a Chinese hamburger, a Chinese meat burger, or a Chinese pork sandwich.
roujiamo.calories: About 400-600 kcal depending on the cut, since the classic version is built on fatty pork belly.
roujiamo.originShort: Xi'an, with roots reaching back to the Qin Dynasty (221-206 BC), which makes it a strong candidate for the world's oldest sandwich.
roujiamo.firstTimer: Yes - mild, filling, cheap (¥8-20), and sold on practically every street in Xi'an.

shengjianbao.title: Shengjian Bao (生煎包): Shanghai Pan-Fried Pork Buns
shengjianbao.description: Shanghai's pan-fried pork buns: crisp golden bottoms, fluffy tops, and a pocket of hot broth. What they cost, how to eat them safely, and where to find them.
shengjianbao.whatIsIt: Shengjian bao are Shanghai pork buns fried in a wide flat pan, giving them crisp golden bottoms, pillowy steamed tops, and a pocket of hot broth inside.
shengjianbao.howToSay: shēng jiān bāo - 3 syllables, said roughly like shung-jyen-bao.
shengjianbao.alsoSpelled: sheng jian bao · shengjianbao · shengjian bao · 生煎包
shengjianbao.inEnglish: In English they are called pan-fried pork buns, Shanghai pan-fried buns, or fried soup buns.
shengjianbao.calories: About 60-90 kcal per bun, so a standard order of four lands around 250-350 kcal.
shengjianbao.originShort: Shanghai street markets in the early 1900s, reportedly when a tea-house cook pan-fried dumplings instead of steaming them.
shengjianbao.firstTimer: Yes - but wait two minutes before your first bite. The broth is trapped under pressure and the bottom is still sizzling when it reaches the table.

mala-tang.title: Mala Tang (麻辣烫): Build-Your-Own Sichuan Hot Pot
mala-tang.description: Build-your-own Sichuan hot pot: pick your ingredients and the cook boils them in numbing mala broth. Pricing rules and how to set your spice level.
mala-tang.whatIsIt: Mala tang is DIY hot pot in a single bowl: you fill a basket from a refrigerated display and the cook boils your selection in numbing-spicy mala broth.
mala-tang.howToSay: má là tàng - 3 syllables, said roughly like mah-lah-tahng.
mala-tang.alsoSpelled: mala tang · malatang · ma la tang · 麻辣烫
mala-tang.inEnglish: In English it is loosely called Sichuan hot pot soup or numbing spicy soup - there is no settled English name for it.
mala-tang.calories: Entirely up to your basket. A vegetable-and-tofu bowl runs 300-500 kcal, while a noodle-heavy bowl with meat easily passes 800.
mala-tang.originShort: Sichuan boatmen on the Yangtze in the 19th century, who boiled skewers in a communal pot of spiced broth to stay warm.
mala-tang.firstTimer: Yes - it is the most forgiving hot pot format, because the cook controls the spice level and you pay by weight rather than by dish.

baocai.title: Paocai (泡菜): Sichuan Pickled Vegetables, Explained
baocai.description: Sichuan pickled vegetables, explained: what paocai (also spelled baocai) is, why it arrives free, how spicy it is, and how it fits into a Sichuan meal.
baocai.whatIsIt: Paocai is Sichuan-style pickled vegetables: cabbage, radish, and carrot cured in a brine with Sichuan peppercorns and chili, almost always served free as a side dish.
baocai.howToSay: pào cài - 2 syllables, said roughly like pow-tsai.
baocai.alsoSpelled: paocai · baocai · pao cai · bao cai · 泡菜 (this page's URL uses 'baocai'; the standard romanisation is 'paocai')
baocai.inEnglish: In English it is called Sichuan pickles, pickled vegetables, or Chinese pickled cabbage.
baocai.calories: Very low - roughly 15-30 kcal for a small serving, since the brine carries salt rather than calories.
baocai.originShort: Sichuan households, with more than 2,000 years of home pickling in water-sealed ceramic jars.
baocai.firstTimer: Yes - it is the mildest thing on a Sichuan table and it arrives free, which makes it a safe reset between spicy dishes.

liangpi.title: Liangpi (凉皮): Xi'an Cold Skin Noodles, Explained
liangpi.description: Xi'an cold skin noodles, explained: what they are made from, what they taste like, what they cost (¥8-18), and how to order them without chili if you prefer.
liangpi.whatIsIt: Liangpi are cold noodles made from wheat or rice starch - wide, translucent, and slippery - tossed with cucumber, bean sprouts, chili oil, vinegar, and sesame paste.
liangpi.howToSay: liáng pí - 2 syllables, said roughly like lyahng-pee.
liangpi.alsoSpelled: liang pi · liangpi · liang fen (a related dish) · 凉皮
liangpi.inEnglish: In English they are called cold skin noodles, Xi'an cold noodles, or Chinese cold noodles.
liangpi.calories: About 300-450 kcal per bowl, mostly from starch and sesame paste, with very little protein.
liangpi.originShort: Xi'an, said to date back to the Qin Dynasty, and still the city's defining summer dish.
liangpi.firstTimer: Yes - ask for it 'bu yao la' (no chili) if you want it mild, and the sesame-vinegar version is refreshing rather than hot.

dan-dan-mian.title: Dan Dan Noodles (担担面): Chengdu's Spicy Sesame Noodles
dan-dan-mian.description: Chengdu's signature noodles, explained: sesame paste, chili oil, Sichuan pepper, and minced pork, mixed at the table. What it costs and how to order it mild.
dan-dan-mian.whatIsIt: Dan dan mian is a Chengdu noodle bowl: thin wheat noodles under sesame paste, chili oil, Sichuan pepper, minced pork, and preserved vegetables, all mixed together at the table.
dan-dan-mian.howToSay: dàn dàn miàn - 3 syllables, said roughly like dan-dan-myen.
dan-dan-mian.alsoSpelled: dan dan mian · dandanmian · dan dan noodles · 担担面
dan-dan-mian.inEnglish: In English it is almost always still called dan dan noodles, sometimes glossed as Sichuan sesame noodles.
dan-dan-mian.calories: About 500-700 kcal per bowl, since the sesame paste and minced pork carry most of the weight.
dan-dan-mian.originShort: Chengdu, named after the bamboo carrying poles ('dan dan') that street vendors balanced their baskets on.
dan-dan-mian.firstTimer: Order it mild ('wei la') the first time. Authentic versions are genuinely numbing, and the sesame base makes the dish richer than it looks.

bingfen.title: Bingfen (冰粉): Sichuan Ice Jelly & Bingfen Seeds
bingfen.description: Sichuan ice jelly, explained: what bingfen is, what it is made from, what it tastes like, and why it is the cold dessert locals eat to recover from hot pot.
bingfen.whatIsIt: Bingfen is a translucent cold jelly made from ice-plant seeds, served in brown-sugar syrup with crushed peanuts, raisins, and sesame seeds.
bingfen.howToSay: bīng fěn - 2 syllables, said roughly like bing-fun.
bingfen.alsoSpelled: bing fen · bingfen · ice jelly · bingfen seeds · 冰粉
bingfen.inEnglish: In English it is called Sichuan ice jelly. It is sometimes confused with grass jelly, which is darker, firmer, and a different dessert altogether.
bingfen.calories: Very light - roughly 100-180 kcal per bowl, most of it the brown-sugar syrup and the nuts.
bingfen.originShort: Sichuan, hundreds of years ago, when villagers discovered that ice-plant seed gum sets into jelly without refrigeration.
bingfen.firstTimer: Yes - it is sweet, cold, and mild, and it is the standard way locals cool their mouths down in the middle of a hot pot meal.

yangrou-chuan.title: Lamb Skewers (羊肉串): Xinjiang Cumin Yangrou Chuan
yangrou-chuan.description: Xinjiang-style lamb skewers, explained: what yangrou chuan are, how they are grilled, what they cost (¥3-8), and where to find the best ones in Xi'an.
yangrou-chuan.whatIsIt: Yangrou chuan are Xinjiang-style lamb skewers: cubes of lamb and fat threaded onto flat metal skewers, grilled over charcoal, and dusted with cumin, chili, and salt.
yangrou-chuan.howToSay: yáng ròu chuàn - 3 syllables, said roughly like yahng-roe-chwan.
yangrou-chuan.alsoSpelled: yang rou chuan · yangrouchuan · lamb skewers · 羊肉串
yangrou-chuan.inEnglish: In English they are called lamb skewers, cumin lamb skewers, or Xinjiang lamb kebabs.
yangrou-chuan.calories: About 60-100 kcal per skewer, so a typical order of five lands around 350-500 kcal.
yangrou-chuan.originShort: Xinjiang, carried east along the Silk Road and absorbed into Xi'an's Muslim Quarter cooking.
yangrou-chuan.firstTimer: Yes - mild, portable, and among the cheapest hot food you will find, at ¥3-8 a skewer.

zhajiangmian.title: Zhajiangmian (炸酱面): Beijing's Signature Noodles
zhajiangmian.description: Beijing's signature noodles, explained: thick wheat noodles, pork-belly soybean sauce, and cool cucumber. What it costs, how to eat it, and where to find it.
zhajiangmian.whatIsIt: Zhajiangmian is Beijing's signature noodle dish: thick wheat noodles under a dark, savoury sauce of fermented soybean paste fried with diced pork belly, plus cool cucumber and radish shreds.
zhajiangmian.howToSay: zhá jiàng miàn - 3 syllables, said roughly like jah-jyahng-myen.
zhajiangmian.alsoSpelled: zhajiang mian · zhajiangmian · zha jiang mian · 炸酱面
zhajiangmian.inEnglish: In English it is called Beijing fried-sauce noodles or noodles with soybean sauce, though most menus simply keep the name zhajiangmian.
zhajiangmian.calories: About 550-750 kcal per bowl. The pork-belly sauce is rich, and the cucumber and radish are the only light part.
zhajiangmian.originShort: Beijing, recorded in Qing Dynasty imperial kitchen notes, where it was reportedly a favourite of Empress Dowager Cixi.
zhajiangmian.firstTimer: Yes - it is not spicy, and the cool vegetable toppings make it the easiest Beijing noodle dish for a first-timer.

mapo-doufu.title: Mapo Tofu (麻婆豆腐): Chengdu's Numbing Tofu Dish
mapo-doufu.description: Chengdu's numbing tofu dish, explained: doubanjiang, fermented black beans, and Sichuan pepper. How spicy it really is, what it costs, and how to order it.
mapo-doufu.whatIsIt: Mapo tofu is diced tofu simmered in a numbing-spicy sauce of doubanjiang chili paste, fermented black beans, and Sichuan peppercorns, usually with a little minced pork.
mapo-doufu.howToSay: má pó dòu fǔ - 4 syllables, said roughly like mah-poe-doe-foo.
mapo-doufu.alsoSpelled: mapo doufu · mapo tofu · ma po tofu · 麻婆豆腐
mapo-doufu.inEnglish: In English it is called mapo tofu, occasionally translated as 'pockmarked grandmother's tofu' after the dish's origin story.
mapo-doufu.calories: About 300-450 kcal per restaurant portion, and you can ask for it without pork to make it lighter and fully vegetarian.
mapo-doufu.originShort: Chengdu, 1862, created at the restaurant now known as Chen Mapo Tofu.
mapo-doufu.firstTimer: Only if you like heat - this is genuinely spicy and numbing. Order it with steamed rice and ask for 'wei la' to tone it down.

xiaomian.title: Chongqing Xiaomian (重庆小面): China's Spiciest Noodles
xiaomian.description: Chongqing's cheap breakfast noodles, explained: chili oil, Sichuan pepper, sesame paste, and minced pork. How spicy it really is and what a bowl costs.
xiaomian.whatIsIt: Xiaomian are Chongqing's cheap breakfast noodles: thin wheat noodles in a dark, fiery dressing of chili oil, Sichuan pepper, sesame paste, vinegar, and minced pork.
xiaomian.howToSay: chóng qìng xiǎo miàn - 4 syllables, said roughly like chong-ching-shyow-myen.
xiaomian.alsoSpelled: xiao mian · xiaomian · chongqing noodles · 重庆小面
xiaomian.inEnglish: In English they are called Chongqing small noodles or Chongqing spicy noodles.
xiaomian.calories: About 450-600 kcal per bowl. The portion is small, but the chili oil and minced pork make it calorie-dense.
xiaomian.originShort: Chongqing's docks, where porters needed fast, cheap, high-energy food before hauling loads up the city's steep streets.
xiaomian.firstTimer: Not if you are heat-shy - this is the spiciest noodle dish on this site. If you do try it, ask for 'wei la' and keep a cold soy milk nearby.

cheong-fun.title: Cheong Fun (肠粉): Cantonese Steamed Rice Noodle Rolls
cheong-fun.description: Cantonese rice noodle rolls, explained: steamed to order on cloth, rolled, and dressed with sweet soy. What they cost and how to order them.
cheong-fun.whatIsIt: Cheong fun are Cantonese rice-noodle rolls: a thin rice sheet steamed to order on cloth, rolled, sliced, and dressed with sweet soy sauce, plain or filled with shrimp, beef, or char siu.
cheong-fun.howToSay: cheong fun in Cantonese, cháng fěn in Mandarin - said roughly like cheung-fun.
cheong-fun.alsoSpelled: chang fen · cheung fun · cheong fun · rice noodle roll · 肠粉
cheong-fun.inEnglish: In English they are called rice noodle rolls, steamed rice rolls, or Cantonese rice noodle rolls.
cheong-fun.calories: About 150-250 kcal for a plain roll, rising toward 350 once you add shrimp or char siu.
cheong-fun.originShort: Guangzhou teahouses in the late Qing Dynasty, where it became a way for chefs to show off their control of texture.
cheong-fun.firstTimer: Yes - very mild, cheap (¥8-20), and a fixture of both Cantonese breakfast and dim sum.

dan-ta.title: Egg Tart (蛋挞): Guangzhou's Flaky Custard Tart
dan-ta.description: Guangzhou's flaky custard tart, explained: how it differs from Portugal's pastel de nata, when to buy it fresh, and what a good one should taste like.
dan-ta.whatIsIt: The Cantonese egg tart is a flaky pastry shell filled with a lightly sweet, wobbling egg custard, a descendant of Portugal's pastel de nata by way of Macau.
dan-ta.howToSay: dàn tà - 2 syllables, said roughly like dan-tah.
dan-ta.alsoSpelled: dan ta · danta · dan tat (Cantonese) · egg tart · 蛋挞
dan-ta.inEnglish: In English it is called an egg tart, a Cantonese egg tart, or a Chinese custard tart.
dan-ta.calories: About 150-200 kcal each, with the pastry making up the heavier half.
dan-ta.originShort: Portugal to Macau in the 16th century, then on to Guangzhou, where bakers made the custard lighter and less sweet.
dan-ta.firstTimer: Yes - it is sweet, mild, and inexpensive (¥5-12). Buy it warm, ideally straight from an afternoon batch.

hongyou-chaoshou.title: Hongyou Chaoshou (红油抄手): Chengdu Chili Oil Wontons
hongyou-chaoshou.description: Chengdu's chili oil wontons, explained: what chaoshou means, how the bowl is built, what it costs, and how to order a mild clear-soup version instead.
hongyou-chaoshou.whatIsIt: Hongyou chaoshou are Chengdu's wontons: small pork dumplings folded 'crossed hands' style and served swimming in fragrant red chili oil, garlic, and black vinegar.
hongyou-chaoshou.howToSay: hóng yóu chāo shǒu - 4 syllables, said roughly like hong-yo-chow-show.
hongyou-chaoshou.alsoSpelled: hong you chaoshou · chaoshou · chao shou · wontons in chili oil · 红油抄手
hongyou-chaoshou.inEnglish: In English they are called wontons in chili oil, Sichuan chili-oil wontons, or red oil wontons.
hongyou-chaoshou.calories: About 350-500 kcal for a bowl of ten. The chili oil is generous even though the wontons themselves are light.
hongyou-chaoshou.originShort: Chengdu in the 1940s, popularised by the Long Chaoshou restaurant on Chunxi Road.
hongyou-chaoshou.firstTimer: Yes if you can take moderate heat. If not, every shop also serves qingtang chaoshou - the same wontons in a clear mild broth.

yangrou-paomo.title: Yangrou Paomo (羊肉泡馍): Xi'an Lamb Soup with Bread
yangrou-paomo.description: Xi'an's lamb and bread soup, explained: why you tear the flatbread yourself, how small the pieces should be, what it costs, and the ritual behind it.
yangrou-paomo.whatIsIt: Yangrou paomo is Xi'an's winter ritual dish: you tear a round of dense flatbread into pea-sized pieces yourself, and the kitchen cooks it in rich lamb broth with vermicelli and tender meat.
yangrou-paomo.howToSay: yáng ròu pào mó - 4 syllables, said roughly like yahng-roe-pow-mwaw.
yangrou-paomo.alsoSpelled: yang rou paomo · paomo · yangrou paomo · lamb paomo · 羊肉泡馍
yangrou-paomo.inEnglish: In English it is called lamb soup with torn bread or Xi'an lamb and bread soup - there is no standard translation.
yangrou-paomo.calories: About 600-800 kcal per bowl. Dense bread plus rich lamb broth makes this the heaviest dish on this site.
yangrou-paomo.originShort: Xi'an's Muslim community, with roots reaching back to the Tang Dynasty (618-907).
yangrou-paomo.firstTimer: Yes - it is not spicy, but budget 45 minutes. The bread-tearing is the whole point, and pieces torn too large can get sent back to the kitchen.

congyoubing.title: Congyoubing (葱油饼): Shanghai Scallion Pancake
congyoubing.description: Shanghai's scallion pancake, explained: how the layers are made, why it is not always vegetarian, what it costs, and when to buy the crispest batch.
congyoubing.whatIsIt: Congyoubing is a scallion pancake: dough rolled paper-thin, layered with chopped scallion and pork fat, coiled into a spiral, flattened, and griddled into dozens of flaky layers.
congyoubing.howToSay: cōng yóu bǐng - 3 syllables, said roughly like tsong-yo-bing.
congyoubing.alsoSpelled: cong you bing · congyoubing · scallion pancake · 葱油饼
congyoubing.inEnglish: In English it is called a scallion pancake, a green onion pancake, or a Chinese spring onion flatbread.
congyoubing.calories: About 250-400 kcal per pancake, since the dough is laminated with rendered pork fat, which is exactly what makes it flaky.
congyoubing.originShort: Northern China, with written records going back to the Northern Wei Dynasty (386-534 AD).
congyoubing.firstTimer: Yes - mild, cheap (¥5-12), and a classic Shanghai breakfast. Note that the traditional recipe uses pork fat, so it is not vegetarian by default.

wonton-noodles.title: Wonton Noodles (云吞面): Cantonese Wonton Soup Guide
wonton-noodles.description: Cantonese wonton noodles, explained: whole-shrimp wontons, springy egg noodles, and a crystal-clear broth. What a bowl costs and how to order it properly.
wonton-noodles.whatIsIt: Wonton noodles are Cantonese comfort food: springy alkaline egg noodles and whole-shrimp wontons in a crystal-clear broth simmered for hours from pork bones, dried flounder, and shrimp shells.
wonton-noodles.howToSay: yún tūn miàn in Mandarin, wan tan min in Cantonese - said roughly like yoon-toon-myen.
wonton-noodles.alsoSpelled: wonton mee · wantan mee · wonton mian · 云吞面
wonton-noodles.inEnglish: In English it is called wonton noodle soup, or Cantonese wonton soup with noodles.
wonton-noodles.calories: About 400-550 kcal per bowl. The portion is deliberately small, which makes it a snack rather than a full meal.
wonton-noodles.originShort: Northern China originally, then completely rebuilt by Cantonese cooks in Guangzhou, where Mak's Noodle has been serving it since the 1920s.
wonton-noodles.firstTimer: Yes - very mild, and the small bowl (¥12-30) makes it easy to try alongside other dishes.

shrimp-dumplings.title: Har Gow (虾饺): Cantonese Shrimp Dumplings, Explained
shrimp-dumplings.description: Cantonese shrimp dumplings, explained: the translucent wrapper, the thirteen pleats, what they cost, and why har gow is the first thing to order at dim sum.
shrimp-dumplings.whatIsIt: Har gow are the benchmark dim sum dumpling: a translucent wheat-starch wrapper pleated around whole shrimp and bamboo shoot, steamed until the pink shrimp shows through.
shrimp-dumplings.howToSay: xiā jiǎo in Mandarin, ha gow in Cantonese - said roughly like shyah-jyow.
shrimp-dumplings.alsoSpelled: har gow · ha gow · xia jiao · shrimp dumplings · 虾饺
shrimp-dumplings.inEnglish: In English they are called shrimp dumplings or Cantonese shrimp dumplings, though dim sum menus almost always keep the name har gow.
shrimp-dumplings.calories: About 40-60 kcal per dumpling, so a standard steamer of four is roughly 200 kcal.
shrimp-dumplings.originShort: Guangzhou's riverside teahouses in the early 20th century, where a chef competed using a translucent wheat-starch wrapper.
shrimp-dumplings.firstTimer: Yes - mild, and it is the traditional first order at dim sum: if the har gow is good, the rest of the kitchen usually is too.
